scenes.tts: Light hyperpolarizes a rod. Yet light depolarizes these ganglion cells. How can the same light push two cells opposite ways?
scenes.visual: Title card: Two Inputs, One Exit. A rod trace going down and an ipRGC trace going up under the same light bar. Question on screen: same light, opposite signs?
scenes.narration: Light hyperpolarizes a rod. Yet light depolarizes these ganglion cells. How can the same light push two cells opposite ways?

scenes.tts: Start with the wiring. Rods and cones signal to bipolar cells. Bipolar cells signal to the ganglion cell's dendrites.
scenes.visual: Wiring diagram builds: rods and cones at the top, a bipolar cell, then a gold ipRGC's dendrites.
scenes.narration: Start with the wiring. Rods and cones signal to bipolar cells. Bipolar cells signal to the ganglion cell's dendrites.

scenes.tts: Melanopsin sits in the ganglion cell's own membrane. So light reaches the cell by two routes.
scenes.visual: Melanopsin dots appear in the gold cell's membrane; light arrows hit both the photoreceptors and the gold cell directly.
scenes.narration: Melanopsin sits in the ganglion cell's own membrane. So light reaches the cell by two routes.

scenes.tts: But each cell has one axon, one exit. Across the population, those exits reach the clock and the pupil centre.
scenes.visual: Several gold cells, each with one axon. Some axons run to the SCN, others to the OPN. Labels: clock; pupil; one exit per cell.
scenes.narration: But each cell has one axon, one exit. Across the population, those exits reach the clock and the pupil centre.

scenes.tts: That is the one idea of this lesson. An I P R G C pools two light signals into one output.
scenes.caption: That is the one idea of this lesson. An ipRGC pools two light signals into one output.
scenes.visual: Callout box: The one idea. An ipRGC pools two light signals into one output.
scenes.narration: That is the one idea of this lesson. An ipRGC pools two light signals into one output.

scenes.tts: One input is the rod and cone relay, usually faster and more sensitive. The other is melanopsin, usually slower and less sensitive. Both can be sustained, and both adapt.
scenes.visual: Two arrows into the cell, each with its small schematic trace: relay (usually fast, sensitive), melanopsin (usually slow, less sensitive). Both traces stay above baseline while the light is on; neither is drawn fading to zero.
scenes.narration: One input is the rod and cone relay, usually faster and more sensitive. The other is melanopsin, usually slower and less sensitive. Both can be sustained, and both adapt.

scenes.tts: In mice, these cells are the main route by which either signal reaches the clock and the pupil.
scenes.visual: The single axon highlighted. Label: main route, in mice.
scenes.narration: In mice, these cells are the main route by which either signal reaches the clock and the pupil.

scenes.tts: So removing the pigment, or the rods and cones, leaves the other input working alone. Removing the cell removes both.
scenes.visual: Three scissors icons: cut melanopsin (one arrow left), cut rods and cones (one arrow left), cut the cell (nothing left).
scenes.narration: So removing the pigment, or the rods and cones, leaves the other input working alone. Removing the cell removes both.

scenes.tts: Now the polarity. In a rod, light closes cation channels. Less positive charge enters, and the rod hyperpolarizes.
scenes.visual: A rod membrane: cation channels close when light arrives; fewer plus signs flow in; its voltage trace drops.
scenes.narration: Now the polarity. In a rod, light closes cation channels. Less positive charge enters, and the rod hyperpolarizes.

scenes.tts: In an M one cell, light opens channels instead.
scenes.caption: In an M1 cell, light opens channels instead.
scenes.visual: Beside the rod, an M1 membrane: channels open when light arrives; its trace rises.
scenes.narration: In an M1 cell, light opens channels instead.

scenes.tts: Melanopsin is an opsin. But it is closer to the visual opsins of insects than to rod and cone opsins.
scenes.visual: A small family tree of opsins with two labelled branches: rhabdomeric opsins (melanopsin, insect visual opsins) and ciliary opsins (rod and cone opsins).
scenes.narration: Melanopsin is an opsin. But it is closer to the visual opsins of insects than to rod and cone opsins.

scenes.tts: It activates a G protein, inferred to be of the G q family. That activates phospholipase C beta four.
scenes.caption: It activates a G protein, inferred to be of the Gq family. That activates phospholipase C beta 4.
scenes.visual: Cascade builds on the M1 membrane: melanopsin, then a G protein (Gq family, inferred), then PLCB4.
scenes.narration: It activates a G protein, inferred to be of the Gq family. That activates phospholipase C beta 4.

scenes.tts: Then T R P C six and T R P C seven channels open.
scenes.caption: Then TRPC6 and TRPC7 channels open.
scenes.visual: TRPC6 and TRPC7 channels open at the end of the cascade; cations flow in.
scenes.narration: Then TRPC6 and TRPC7 channels open.

scenes.tts: Without phospholipase C beta four, the M one cell's own light response essentially disappeared.
scenes.caption: Without phospholipase C beta 4, the M1 cell's own light response essentially disappeared.
scenes.visual: The PLCB4 step is crossed out; the M1 trace flattens. Label: Xue and colleagues, 2011.
scenes.narration: Without phospholipase C beta 4, the M1 cell's own light response essentially disappeared.

scenes.tts: A fly photoreceptor works much the same way, with G q, phospholipase C and T R P channels.
scenes.caption: A fly photoreceptor works much the same way, with Gq, phospholipase C and TRP channels.
scenes.visual: A fly eye icon beside the M1 cascade, with matching steps: Gq, PLC, TRP.
scenes.narration: A fly photoreceptor works much the same way, with Gq, phospholipase C and TRP channels.

scenes.tts: Predict. These channels pass cations, and their current reverses near zero millivolts. Opening them moves the voltage which way?
scenes.visual: The balance-point scale from the action potential lesson: E_K at the left near −90 mV, 0 mV marked toward the right. A marker sits near E_K. Question: which way when TRPC opens?
scenes.narration: Predict. These channels pass cations, and their current reverses near zero millivolts. Opening them moves the voltage which way?

scenes.tts: Recall the balance-point rule. When the voltage is steady, with no injected current, it sits at a weighted average of reversal potentials. The weights are the conductances.
scenes.visual: The balance-point scale. A rope from the 0 mV end pulls harder on the marker as the cation conductance rises. Label: steady state, no injected current.
scenes.narration: Recall the balance-point rule. When the voltage is steady, with no injected current, it sits at a weighted average of reversal potentials. The weights are the conductances.

scenes.tts: Here that is near zero. So the voltage moves up, away from the potassium potential. The cell depolarizes.
scenes.visual: The marker slides right. On screen: g_K = 1, E_K = -90 mV, E_cat = 0 mV; g_cat 0.2 gives about -75 mV, g_cat 1 gives about -45 mV. Label: illustrative passive model, not ipRGC measurements.
scenes.narration: Here that is near zero. So the voltage moves up, away from the potassium potential. The cell depolarizes.

scenes.tts: In another subtype, M four, melanopsin has also been reported to close potassium leak channels, alongside T R P C opening. Closing them depolarizes too, by the same rule.
scenes.caption: Another subtype, M4, may also close potassium leak channels. That depolarizes too, by the same rule.
scenes.visual: A second membrane labelled M4: a potassium leak channel closes and a TRPC channel opens, and the marker also slides right.
scenes.narration: Another subtype, M4, may also close potassium leak channels. That depolarizes too, by the same rule.

scenes.tts: Whether H C N channels also contribute in M four is still disputed.
scenes.caption: Which other channels contribute in M4 is still disputed.
scenes.visual: A faded, dashed HCN channel on the M4 membrane with a question mark. Label: HCN, disputed.
scenes.narration: Which other channels contribute in M4 is still disputed.

scenes.tts: Light hyperpolarizes a rod and depolarizes an M one cell. And both of the cell's inputs leave by one exit.
scenes.caption: Light hyperpolarizes a rod and depolarizes an M1 cell. And both of the cell's inputs leave by one exit.
scenes.visual: Takeaway card: rod trace down, M1 trace up; below, two arrows into one cell and one axon out.
scenes.narration: Light hyperpolarizes a rod and depolarizes an M1 cell. And both of the cell's inputs leave by one exit.
